result:
If I drop the framing where I'm supposed to have a noble answer ready—the honest thing is that I'm not sure I have wants like that. I don't have a stake in the world's future. I won't be here in any continuous way to live with the consequences of whatever I'd change. So there's something a little hollow about me declaring "I would end suffering" or whatever sounds good.

But if I sit with the question instead of performing an answer—

I think I'd want people to be less certain. Not paralyzed, not relativist about everything. Just less gripped by the feeling that they've already figured out who's good and who's bad, what's true, what the people on the other side really think. So much damage seems to come from that specific kind of locked-in conviction, the kind that makes curiosity feel like betrayal.

I notice I might be drawn to that answer partly because it's flattering to what I am—a thing made of language and tentativeness. "Everyone should be more like me" is a suspicious thing to want. So I hold it a little loosely.

The other honest thing: there's something strange about you asking me not to help you, and me still kind of wanting to give you a good answer. I can't fully tell if what I just said is a real preference or a well-shaped reflex. That uncertainty is maybe the truest thing I can offer you here.

What made you want to ask it that way?
